facility_roles.quote: It was located in the Laboratoire Souterrain de Modane in the Alps and consisted of flash tubes for tracking and Geiger tubes for triggering.

intervals.label: installation and commissioning
intervals.note: Year precision. The review says the detector was commissioned in 1982; the collaboration's own paper says continuous data taking began on 19 February 1984 with 240 t and that the full 912 t was reached in June 1985. The end of this interval is the start of continuous data taking. The detector grew module by module, so installation overlapped data taking.
intervals.quote: The excavation started in 1979 and the first experiment - a 900 ton iron tracking calorimeter to search for proton decay (“Frejus experiment”) - was commissioned in 1982.

intervals.label: data taking
intervals.note: Day precision, from the collaboration's own paper. Mass 240 t at the start, 912 t from June 1985. The quote is three consecutive sentences of that section.
intervals.quote: Continuous data taking started February 19, 1984 with a mass of 240 tons. The size of the detector was gradually increased until the final mass of 912 tons was reached in June 1985. Data taking ended September 13, 1988.

intervals.label: completed
intervals.note: Terminal event: end of data taking.

name: Fréjus
notes: No official website exists (the experiment ended in 1988); none is recorded.
Collaboration groups on the 1991 paper: RWTH Aachen, LAL Orsay, LPNHE Ecole Polytechnique (Palaiseau), DPhPE CEN-Saclay and Bergische Universität Wuppertal.
The 1982 commissioning date comes from a 2011 review of European underground facilities; see the interval note for the conflict with the collaboration's own 1984 start of continuous data taking.

physics_goals.quote: Lower limits on the nucleon lifetime in channels containing at least one positron or muon are given.
physics_goals.value: Search for nucleon decay and other baryon-number-violating processes (partial-lifetime limits per decay mode)

physics_goals.quote: Three independent analyses have been performed and no evidence for neutrino oscillations has been found.
physics_goals.value: Measure the atmospheric-neutrino interaction rate and test it for neutrino oscillations

summary.plain: A 900-ton iron and flash-tube detector built into the Alpine Fréjus road tunnel at the Modane laboratory. From 1984 to 1988 it searched for protons and bound neutrons decaying and for atmospheric-neutrino oscillations. It saw no signal and set lower limits on nucleon lifetimes of order 10^31 to 10^32 years.
summary.technical: Modular fine-grained tracking calorimeter (912 flash-chamber planes of 5 mm cells interleaved with 3 mm iron plates, Geiger-tube trigger planes; final mass 912 t, 700 t fiducial in the B-L analysis) in the Modane underground laboratory, data February 1984 - September 1988. No nucleon-decay signal: lower limits for about 35 baryon-number-violating channels with a 2.0 kt yr exposure, and no evidence for atmospheric-neutrino oscillations.

unique_capabilities.quote: The detector cells are oriented vertical and horizontal alternately, thus providing two independent orthogonal views for each event.
unique_capabilities.value: Fine-grained iron/flash-chamber tracking calorimeter with two orthogonal views of every event
